title: Once-Weekly HIV Pill Matches Daily Therapy in Landmark Trials, Paving Way for First Oral Long-Acting Treatment
excerpt: A combination of islatravir and lenacapavir suppressed HIV as effectively as daily Biktarvy in two Phase 3 trials, with zero patients on the weekly pill showing detectable virus at 48 weeks.
body:
• A once-weekly pill combining islatravir and lenacapavir matched the efficacy of daily HIV medication in two Phase 3 trials involving more than 600 patients across 12 countries.
  • Zero patients on the weekly pill had detectable viral levels at 48 weeks, compared with 0.3% on the leading daily treatment Biktarvy.
  • Gilead Sciences and Merck plan to file for regulatory approval globally, with the combination potentially becoming the first approved once-weekly oral HIV treatment.
  • The results were published in The New England Journal of Medicine and presented at the International AIDS Conference (AIDS 2026).

A single pill taken once a week kept HIV suppressed as effectively as the best daily regimen available, according to results from two pivotal clinical trials that researchers say could fundamentally change how the virus is managed worldwide.

The Weekly Pill

The experimental treatment combines two long-acting antiretroviral drugs — Merck's islatravir, a next-generation nucleoside analog, and Gilead's lenacapavir, a first-in-class capsid inhibitor already approved under the brand name Yeztugo for twice-yearly injectable prevention. Together, their pharmacokinetic profiles enable effective dosing in a single tablet taken just once a week.

The combination was tested in two Phase 3 trials — ISLEND-1 and ISLEND-2 — involving adults whose HIV was already controlled on daily antiretroviral therapy. ISLEND-1 enrolled patients switching from Gilead's daily Biktarvy, while ISLEND-2 drew from patients on various standard daily regimens.

"The first ever weekly oral therapy for the treatment of HIV could offer welcome relief from the burden of lifelong daily pill-taking for people living with HIV."

— Chloe Orkin, Dean for Healthcare Transformation, Queen Mary University of London

Trial Results

In ISLEND-1, none of the patients who switched to the weekly pill had detectable viral levels at 48 weeks — compared with 0.3% of those who stayed on Biktarvy. In ISLEND-2, just 0.3% of patients taking the weekly pill had detectable HIV levels, compared with 1.3% on standard daily regimens. The weekly treatment met the statistical bar for non-inferiority in both studies.

Side effects were generally comparable to existing daily treatments. The most common treatment-related effects included headache, nausea, and diarrhea. No new safety concerns emerged, according to data presented at the 26th International AIDS Conference (AIDS 2026) in July and published in The New England Journal of Medicine.

Why It Matters

Approximately 39 million people worldwide live with HIV, and treatment requires strict adherence to daily medication. Even brief lapses risk viral rebound and the development of drug resistance. While injectable long-acting treatments have gained ground — Gilead's twice-yearly lenacapavir injection and ViiV Healthcare's monthly cabotegravir — many patients prefer oral medication over injections that require clinical visits.

"This is especially important for people that are experiencing stigma and people with other HIV-associated health conditions who are taking multiple other tablets," Orkin said.

The weekly pill could bridge the gap between daily oral therapy and injectable options, offering convenience without the needle. Jürgen Rockstroh of the University Hospital Bonn called the results evidence that "the treatment landscape is evolving" beyond the daily pill paradigm that has defined HIV care for decades.

Road to Approval

Gilead and Merck said they plan to file for regulatory approval globally based on the ISLEND trial data. If approved, the islatravir-lenacapavir combination would become the first once-weekly oral HIV treatment on the market. Separately, the FDA has already accepted Gilead's application for a once-weekly oral formulation of lenacapavir for HIV prevention (PrEP), with a decision expected by February 2027.

The clinical trial will continue to follow participants for 96 weeks total to assess longer-term safety and durability of viral suppression. Investors are closely watching the rollout as Gilead seeks to strengthen its HIV franchise alongside its blockbuster daily treatment Biktarvy, which generated $14.1 billion in revenue last year.

Global Implications

For countries with large HIV populations — including India, which has the third-largest number of people living with HIV worldwide — a weekly oral option could simplify treatment logistics, improve adherence in resource-limited settings, and reduce the stigma associated with daily pill-taking. The combination's dual mechanism of action, targeting HIV at multiple stages of its lifecycle, also offers a potential advantage against resistance development.
